title: The hen and her chicks (Luke 13:31–35)
hookLine: Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem like a hen gathers her brood

lines: A HAWK'S SHADOW ON THE YARD.
cards: When a hawk's shadow crosses the yard, a mother hen moves fast. She calls with a sharp cluck, the chicks run to her, and she spreads her wings and crouches so they disappear underneath.
All you see is one puffed-up bird, staring the danger down. Whatever comes now comes to her first. Jesus is on his long road to Jerusalem when some Pharisees warn him that Herod wants to kill him.
His answer starts with a fox and ends with a hen.

teach.b: First, notice who warns him. Some Pharisees come and say: get out of here, Herod wants to kill you. Not every Pharisee in the Gospels is an opponent, and these seem to be trying to protect him.

Jesus answers: go and tell that fox, today and tomorrow I cast out devils and heal, and on the third day I'm finished. He won't be rushed by a fox. Then his voice turns, and he speaks to a city that isn't there.

"Jerusalem, Jerusalem, that killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent to thee, how often would I have gathered thy children as the bird doth her brood under her wings, and thou wouldest not?"
The Douay says bird. The Greek word can mean any bird, but it was the usual word for a hen, and English Bibles have long said hen.

Not a lion or an eagle, which kings liked. A barnyard mother with nothing to fight with but her own body. Herod is the fox, and Jesus pictures himself as the hen who stands between the fox and the chicks.

teach.h: AS THE BIRD DOTH HER BROOD UNDER HER WINGS.
teach.b: The Psalms already spoke this way about God, asking to be hidden under the shadow of your wings. And notice: and thou wouldest not. A hen can call; she can't make a chick run.
There's grief in this line, not anger. Catholic writers have long loved the image. Saint Anselm wrote a prayer calling Jesus our mother, who gathers us under his wings like a hen.

how: Catholics pray for their cities in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, and many parishes hold processions or vigils through their neighborhoods; Psalm 91, with its shelter under God's wings, is prayed at Night Prayer on Sundays.

games.q: some people warn you that a ruler wants you dead and you should leave. what do you say?
o: thank them and leave town quietly.
tell that fox I'm finishing my work.
games.why: he sends word to Herod that he'll keep healing, then grieves over Jerusalem like a hen longing to gather her chicks.

practice: Picture the place where you live, close up, at street level: the bus stop, the clinic waiting room, the school gate, a doorway where someone sleeps. Let one corner of it come near, and picture wings spread over it.
If you pray, ask God to gather your city under his wings; if you don't, simply hold it in your attention, with care.

wordCard.voice: Hen. Jesus' picture of himself longing to gather Jerusalem under his wings, standing between the fox and the brood. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: bird, and commonly a hen. The word behind the hen of Luke 13:34.

carryVoice: Your line: under her wings. Tender, and strong, and a little surprising. Day four hundred sixty-seven, in the books.
